speaker: Albert Gu
title: No Priors Ep. 70 | With Cartesia Co-Founders Karan Goel & Albert Gu
question: In production voice AI, why do standalone text-to-speech and speech-recognition models hit a quality ceiling that forces teams toward multimodal foundation models?
guest: Even just for your basic evaluations of whether your ASR system can recognize these words or whether your TTS system can say this word, that is actually not quite a local problem. For a lot of hard things, you actually need to have real language understanding in order to process and figure out what is the right way of pronouncing this and so on. So actually, to really get perfect TTS or speech-to-speech, you really need to have a model that has deeper understanding—at least of the language—so it's not really an isolated component anymore. You have to start getting into these multimodal models just to even do one modality well. That's somewhere we were eyeing from the beginning as well, and we're using audio as an entry point into building out the stack toward all of that, which is going to help the audio as well as start getting other modalities in there.

points.core: Accurate pronunciation in speech generation is not a purely local acoustic problem.
points.note: Accept: basic TTS pronunciation or ASR word recognition cannot be solved from local phoneme or acoustic patterns alone. Do not credit: generic claims that audio is noisy or hard to synthesize.

points.core: Hard speech cases require genuine language understanding to resolve context-dependent pronunciation.
points.note: Accept: deciding how to pronounce ambiguous words, homographs, or nuanced phrases requires semantic and linguistic comprehension of broader context. Do not credit: vague mentions of "more training data" or "larger acoustic models" without citing language understanding.

points.core: Speech stops functioning as an isolated component once high-fidelity performance is required.
points.note: Accept: perfecting even a single modality like audio forces teams into joint multimodal language models rather than modular standalone audio components. Do not credit: arguing multimodality is only needed to cut pipeline latency or add extra modalities.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
The ceiling comes from the cascade architecture itself, not from weak individual components. When speech recognition, a language model, and text-to-speech are chained, text becomes the only interface between them, and text is a lossy bottleneck. The recognizer discards tone, emotion, emphasis, hesitation, speaker identity, and overlapping speech, so the language model reasons over a flattened transcript. The synthesizer then has to guess prosody from words alone, without knowing how the user sounded or what the reply is meant to convey, which produces speech that is fluent but contextually off.

Errors also compound: a misheard name or number is passed downstream as fact, and no later stage can go back to the audio to recover. Latency stacks across stages, and natural turn-taking (interruptions, backchannels, knowing when someone has finished) has to be bolted on with separate voice-activity and endpointing heuristics.

Improving each model in isolation cannot fix information that was never passed along. Multimodal models that take in and generate audio natively, with shared context, keep the paralinguistic signal and optimise understanding, reasoning and delivery jointly. The trade-off is that cascades remain easier to control, audit and debug, so many production teams still use them.

The response discusses shared context for prosody but does not explain how understanding meaning resolves ambiguous pronunciation.
The response identifies a speech quality limit that isolated components cannot overcome and explains how joint multimodal modeling preserves the context needed for delivery.
quotes: Improving each model in isolation cannot fix information that was never passed along.
Multimodal models that take in and generate audio natively, with shared context, keep the paralinguistic signal and optimise understanding, reasoning and delivery jointly.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer:
Standalone speech-recognition (ASR) and text-to-speech (TTS) models hit a quality ceiling because routing conversation through a plain-text bottleneck strips away acoustic and paralinguistic meaning. When ASR flattens audio into transcripts, cues like emotion, sarcasm, hesitation, urgency, and acoustic context vanish before reaching the reasoning layer. Downstream, standalone TTS must guess prosody from surface text without deep world knowledge or discourse state, struggling to place natural emphasis, shift tone dynamically, or produce organic non-verbal cues like sighs and laughter.

Cascading separate ASR, LLM, and TTS pipelines also compounds end-to-end latency and propagates errors irreversibly, since a misheard homophone or premature endpoint cutoff corrupts the entire reply. Meanwhile, brittle voice-activity heuristics falter on fluid human turn-taking, backchanneling, and mid-sentence interruptions.

Multimodal foundation models overcome these limits by processing and generating audio natively within a shared representation space. Unifying listening, semantic reasoning, and vocal synthesis end-to-end preserves paralinguistic nuance, cuts response latency, handles natural barge-ins, and grounds vocal expression directly in conversational intent.

points.why: The response describes lost vocal cues and mentions a misheard homophone without explaining why local acoustic or phoneme patterns are insufficient for pronunciation or word recognition.
The response links discourse state to expressive prosody but never explains how language understanding resolves a context-dependent pronunciation.
The response argues that integrating audio and semantic reasoning improves the fidelity of speech by grounding vocal expression in conversational intent.
quotes: Multimodal foundation models overcome these limits by processing and generating audio natively within a shared representation space.
grounds vocal expression directly in conversational intent.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
The ceiling comes from the cascade itself. A standalone ASR → LLM → TTS pipeline passes only text between stages, and text is a lossy bottleneck. ASR throws away prosody, emotion, emphasis, hesitation, speaker identity and background context. The language model then reasons without knowing whether the user sounded sarcastic, confused or urgent. TTS has to guess how to say a reply it didn't write and doesn't fully understand, so it often gets stress, emotion and pacing wrong, especially on names, numbers and code-switched speech.

Errors also compound. A misrecognized word ends up as a confident wrong answer, and no stage can recover what an earlier one discarded. Latency stacks up across the three hops, which makes natural turn-taking, barge-in and backchanneling ("mm-hm") hard. Teams end up hand-tuning endpointing and SSML heuristics, and those plateau.

Speech-native multimodal models keep audio representations end to end. They can condition their answers on how something was said, produce context-appropriate expressiveness, and stream with lower latency. That said, many production systems still use cascades because they're more controllable, cheaper, easier to debug and safer to audit.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer: Standalone speech-recognition and text-to-speech pipelines hit a quality ceiling primarily because text is a lossy bottleneck. When an ASR model transcribes audio into plain text, it strips away prosody, emotion, pacing, hesitation, emphasis, and acoustic context—meaning the downstream language model never actually hears how something was said. On the output side, a standalone TTS model must reconstruct natural delivery from flat text without deep access to conversational intent, often resulting in mismatched tone or robotic cadence. Cascading separate models also compounds errors and latency: a misheard word or domain term propagates unrecoverably into the response, while sequential buffering and rigid endpointing make natural turn-taking, interruptions, and backchanneling feel sluggish. Multimodal foundation models overcome these limits by processing and generating audio natively within a shared representation space. Because acoustic understanding, reasoning, and speech synthesis happen jointly, these models preserve paralinguistic nuance, use broad world knowledge to disambiguate noisy or accented speech, and achieve the low-latency, emotionally responsive flow required for human-like voice interaction.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
Standalone speech recognition and text-to-speech optimize for separate tasks. Recognition turns audio into words, often discarding cues like hesitation, emphasis, and sarcasm. The dialogue model then reasons from that transcript, so a misheard name or a missed cue can change the answer. Text-to-speech only sees the reply it’s given, which limits its ability to match the moment. Each handoff can also add latency, making pauses and interruptions harder to handle naturally.

Multimodal foundation models can use the caller’s audio alongside the conversation history to decide what to say, how to say it, and when to speak. That shared context matters most in open-ended conversations, where tone and timing can change the meaning of the same words. A standalone pipeline can still work well for structured tasks where an accurate transcript captures most of what the system needs.

points.why: The response describes lost conversational cues and misheard names without explaining why pronunciation or word recognition requires information beyond local speech patterns.
The response explains how tone and timing affect meaning without showing how understanding that meaning resolves an ambiguous pronunciation.
The response presents joint modeling as beneficial for open-ended conversation without establishing that high-fidelity speech itself requires moving beyond standalone components.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
Standalone speech recognition and text-to-speech hit a quality ceiling when the transcript becomes the only thing they share. A recognizer can transcribe “I’m fine” perfectly while losing the hesitation that makes it sound doubtful. A synthesizer can pronounce a reply flawlessly, but the words alone may leave its tone, emphasis, and timing ambiguous. Improving word accuracy or voice realism does little to recover cues the system has already discarded.

Multimodal foundation models can learn from speech and text together, using both what someone said and how they said it to shape the response. That matters in live conversation, where a pause can signal either “I’m thinking” or “your turn.” Teams can extend a modular system to pass along acoustic cues, so the shift is a practical pressure rather than a technical necessity.

points.why: The response assumes flawless pronunciation and locates the quality ceiling in lost cues about tone, emphasis, and timing.
The response discusses interpreting pauses and hesitation without explaining how linguistic meaning resolves ambiguous pronunciation.
The response treats joint multimodal modeling as a practical preference and presents passing acoustic cues between modules as a viable alternative.
